title: MB7-15824
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Haiti, alleges that he is a "Convention refugee" and a "person in need of protection," as defined in section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The claimant alleges that politically motivated criminals accused him of leading protests in support of his uncle's return to work; his uncle, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, had been arbitrarily dismissed after XXXX years of service.

On XXXX XXXX, 2010, these criminals went to the claimant's parents' home, but he was not there. They fired projectiles at a dog and in the air, smashed the front door of the house and set tires on fire.
On XXXX XXXX, 2010, the claimant left Haiti and moved to Venezuela.

In 2016, because of the economic crisis in the country and the problems it caused for foreign residents, the claimant fled Venezuela. He travelled through several countries in the Americas before arriving in Canada in XXXX 2017.
The panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection", as there is no credible basis for his claim, for the reasons that follow. ANALYSIS Identity

The claimant's identity was established by means of his birth certificate and a copy of the personal information page of his passport; these documents were seized when his refugee protection claim was received.1 Exclusion under Article 1E The claimant's status in Venezuela

In his Generic Application Form for Canada,2 the claimant alleges that he obtained permanent resident status in Venezuela. Because of that statement, on November 5, 2020, the panel sent a letter to the Minister regarding a possible exclusion under Article 1E. In a letter dated November 17, 2020, the Minister responded that he would not intervene in this case as he had no additional information on the claimant's status in Venezuela. The panel nonetheless analyzed the possibility of exclusion under Article 1E, given the claimant's statements.

When asked about his status in Venezuela, the claimant testified that he had obtained [translation] "permanent residence for five years." That statement, combined with the written statement in the above-mentioned form, creates prima facie evidence that the claimant is a permanent resident of Venezuela.

When asked to provide clearer information about the validity period of his resident status, the claimant explained that his resident status had been indicated in his passport but that the authorities had also issued him an identity card, which he needed to renew every five years. Neither the claimant's passport nor this identity card are on the record, as the claimant allegedly lost them during his trip from Venezuela to Canada.

On reviewing the documentary evidence, the panel notes that resident status in Venezuela is indeed granted for five years: According to sources, the resident visa is valid for five years (Venezuela n.d.e; Retired Professor 27 Feb. 2018; IOM 29 May 2018). Sources state that the resident visa is renewable (UN 9 Mar. 2018; Retired Professor 27 Feb. 2018).3

The process for renewing this status is also described in the documentary evidence. It is an administrative process, in which residents must provide proof of "their identity and their legal status in the country."4 In the panel's opinion, this shows that it is indeed a process for renewing resident status, not simply a process for renewing identity documents.
After analyzing all the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant had a temporary status, as he had to renew it every five years.

The claimant's status was not substantially similar to that of Venezuelan nationals, and the claimant is not excluded from the Convention by operation of Article 1E and of section 98 of the IRPA. Credibility

The claimant's testimony during the hearing was spontaneous and straightforward, and the panel has no reason to doubt his allegations. However, the claimant's testimony during the hearing showed that, if he returned to Haiti, he would not be subjected to a risk in connection with the allegations in his refugee protection claim. Allegations in the Basis of Claim Form

When asked to explain whom he fears in Haiti, the claimant stated that the person he was most afraid of, the leader of the criminal group he fled from, is dead. Then, when asked whom he would fear if he had to return to Haiti, the claimant stated that he cannot return there because of the current situation in the country, especially since he has three children who are now in Canada. When asked if he believes that the gang members who targeted him in the past would have an interest in him, despite the fact that their leader is dead, the claimant answered that the country is [translation] "completely rotten" and that people have been killed in the region he comes from.

In light of the claimant's testimony, the panel concludes, on a balance of probabilities, that the criminals who targeted him in 2010 would no longer have an interest in him, 10 years later and given that their leader is dead. Consequently, the claimant does not face a prospective risk in connection with his allegations regarding this gang. The claimant's allegations at the hearing about the general situation in Haiti

When asked about whether he would face a risk that is different in nature or degree from the risk faced by Haitian residents as a whole, the claimant stated that those people have become resigned to living in the country, whereas he is already in Canada, he has a job here, and the lack of employment and insecurity in Haiti would drive him crazy.

After analyzing all the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant has not established that he would face a personal risk if he returned to Haiti. Consequently, despite the evidence concerning the general insecurity in Haiti, the claimant's allegations in this regard do not support his refugee protection claim. A fear of being a victim of generalized crime cannot give rise to a positive determination under section 96 of the IRPA. Furthermore, given the absence of a personal risk, subsection 97(1) of the IRPA does not apply: It is important that a decision-maker finds that a claimant has a personal risk because if there is no personal risk to the claimant, then there is no need to do any further analysis of the claim; there is simply no risk. It is only after finding that there is a personal risk that a decision-maker must continue to consider whether that risk is one faced generally by the population.5

The panel also notes that the evidence on the general situation in the country is insufficient, on its own, to support a refugee protection claim.6 Submission from the claimant's counsel: members of the diaspora who return to Haiti

During her submissions, the claimant's counsel argued that the claimant, who has been outside his country for 10 years, would be viewed differently from people who have always lived in Haiti and would therefore face a greater risk, since he could be targeted by threats or scams, which creates a risk to his safety.
The panel considered in particular the new Tab 14.1 of the National Documentation Package7 on the risk faced by members of the diaspora who return to Haiti.

It is true that this document states that people returning from North America are perceived, in the common imagination, as having money and could be targeted out of envy. However, the same document states that it is not always obvious that someone has returned from abroad, which certainly mitigates the risk factor: In an interview with the Research Directorate, a Haitian human rights lawyer stated that people returning from abroad are not automatically categorized as such by society in general, because there is no way for their fellow citizens to know that they are returnees, unless there is media coverage; according to him, any [translation] "indexing" is only by their inner circle (Lawyer 17 June 2020).

Furthermore, according to the documentary evidence, violent crime is widespread in Haiti and can affect all citizens in the country at random, regardless of whether or not they are members of the diaspora returning to the country. It is well established in the case law that being a victim of crime does not constitute a ground of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA.8 Similarly, a generalized risk of crime shared by the population as a whole cannot form the basis of a claim for refugee protection under subparagraph 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA.9

Moreover, as Madam Justice Tremblay-Lamer states in Prophète:10 In the recent case of Carias v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 602, [2007] F.C.J. No. 817 (QL), at paras. 23 and 25, O'Keefe J. concluded that the applicants faced a generalized risk of economic crime which was experienced by many other Hondurans, including those perceived as wealthy. In that particular case, the Board accepted that the applicants had been the victims of violence, however, O'Keefe J. dismissed the application indicating, at para. 25, that "[t]he applicants are members of a large group of people who may be targeted for economic crimes in Honduras on basis of their perceived wealth." Further, he held that "[g]iven the wording of subparagraph 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA, the applicants had to satisfy the Board that they would be personally subjected to a risk that was not generally faced by others in Honduras." Based on the recent jurisprudence of this Court, I am of the view that the applicant does not face a personalized risk that is not faced generally by other individuals in or from Haiti. The risk of all forms of criminality is general and felt by all Haitians. While a specific number of individuals may be targeted more frequently because of their wealth, all Haitians are at risk of becoming the victims of violence.11

In addition, in Jean,12 the Federal Court states that "the diaspora as a whole cannot be considered a [translation] 'risk group' and that each case must be considered individually and within [translation] 'its own context.'" The case law also indicates that the claimant must discharge their burden of establishing the specific circumstances that would make the risk they face different in nature or degree from that faced by the population as a whole: The RPD must answer the following question: whether in the context of the alleged present or prospective risks, the applicants provided evidence of their specific circumstances that would make their risk distinct from that of the general population given the widespread presence of gangs in their country.13
In this case, it must be noted that there is no basis for concluding that the claimant would be targeted differently from any other Haitian who is perceived as being wealthy or who attracts envy.

Therefore, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that if he returned to Haiti, he would face a risk that is different in nature or degree than that faced generally by other people in Haiti, by reason of his status as someone returning from a foreign country.

After analyzing all the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant would not face a serious possibility of persecution in Haiti and that, on a balance of probabilities, he would not be personally subjected to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

The panel also finds that there is no credible or trustworthy evidence on which it could have made a favourable decision. The panel concludes that it is clear from the claimant's statements at the hearing that the risk alleged in his Basis of Claim Form no longer exists. Moreover, the allegations regarding the general situation in Haiti, while credible, cannot form a basis for a favourable decision.
The panel determines that the claimant, XXXX XXXX, is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.
The panel finds that the refugee protection claim has no credible basis, in accordance with subsection 107(2) of the IRPA.

Consequently, the panel rejects the claim for refugee protection.
